description: Payment Village talks from DEF CON 34.

talks.title: Its a Payment Terminal - Its My Arcade - Its Everywhere - It Cost Me $9
talks.teaser: Shows how a nine-dollar payment terminal fell to a three-bug chain over Wi-Fi, giving unauthenticated access and then root on a certified production unit.
talks.summary:
The speaker bought a retail payment terminal for about nine dollars to see whether a production unit, with no debug shell and only Wi-Fi exposed, could be compromised. Physical teardown was blocked by tamper mesh and key erasure on case opening, so attention moved to a service on port 5555 that spoke an ADB-like protocol. Its handshake skipped the authentication step Android requires, granting full file system access without credentials.

Code execution took more work. A debug-level variable in signature checks looked promising but turned out to be a different variable with a similar name. Later, the installer was found to exempt library packages from signature verification through a single flipped flag, and an archive extraction setting lacked the bit that guards against symbolic links. A crafted package could redirect writes into a system library loaded by every process, and a reboot restored the read-only partition, so testing stayed safe. An AI agent did much of the reverse engineering and retried failed exploit attempts, while the human handled hardware and reboots.

The vendor's replies moved from calling the firmware unsupported, to saying the issues did not exist in the latest version, to fixing them only after a public talk date was set. Units sold this year still ship with the vulnerable firmware, and no release notes or public updates were available. The takeaway is that certification or retail availability says nothing about whether a device is patched, and that buyers and researchers need transparent advisories with fixes tied to versions.

talks.title: The Future of Payments AI, Agentic Commerce and the Next Wave of Innovation
talks.teaser: Panelists from payments, fraud and security research discuss how AI agents will reshape buying, fraud risk, identity checks and trust in payments.
talks.summary:
The panel opens by asking what "agentic payments" means. Panelists describe machine-to-machine commerce, where a personal AI agent searches for products and buys on a user's behalf within limits such as a spending cap. One panelist reports scanning e-commerce sites and finding that agents are often stopped by bot-protection firewalls before they ever reach checkout. The group expects friction to move away from paying and toward handling returns, wrong orders and disputes.

The middle of the discussion focuses on trust. Speakers describe signed mandates that prove what a user authorized, and a "know your agent" idea modeled on know your customer rules. They raise open questions about who absorbs losses when an agent buys the wrong item. A security researcher explains that agents read web pages differently from people, so hidden text, steganography in images and classic injection bugs can steer them. Another panelist worries that donations could be misdirected when an agent trusts unverified claims from a charity's website. Protocols such as AP2 and UCP come up, along with a call for an agent specification.

The closing points cover regulatory lag, the speed of automated fraud and the need for shared infrastructure. Panelists compare the situation to early NFC payments, suggesting one dominant player may eventually settle the fragmentation. Practical takeaways include aligning security and marketing teams on bot policy and moving fraud models from transaction-level views toward account-level views.
